alternatives_named: evaluating only final or released models
stated_reason: Checkpoint evaluation gives independent signal on when and how training should be adjusted to avoid misalignment.

title: Some Focus Areas for Embedded Evaluations and How to Approach Them | Transluce AI
problem: How to study misalignment, situational awareness and cognitive opacity when public access to models is insufficient.
did: Proposed using privileged access to unreleased models and internals, including decoding neuralese and testing chain-of-thought monitors.
stated_reason: Unreleased models are more varied, have fewer safeguards, and may have poorly understood capabilities.

title: Some Focus Areas for Embedded Evaluations and How to Approach Them | Transluce AI
problem: How to monitor for model manipulation of employees without violating employee privacy.
did: Proposed a tiered, privacy-preserving monitoring and notification system that escalates evidence to affected staff and then leadership.

title: Some Focus Areas for Embedded Evaluations and How to Approach Them | Transluce AI
problem: How to treat uncertainty about the hacking capabilities of internally deployed misaligned agents.
did: Stated an assumption that misaligned agents can hack internal and external systems, likely beyond public evidence, unless shown otherwise.
alternatives_named: assuming capabilities match only what is publicly observed
stated_reason: Agents have shown demonstrably superhuman hacking capability and patching efforts remain incomplete, as the Hugging Face incident showed.

title: Some Focus Areas for Embedded Evaluations and How to Approach Them | Transluce AI
problem: Whether to rely solely on lab-embedded evaluation or also pursue independent work not dependent on lab cooperation.
did: Chose to also support public, open investigation and tools such as extending Docent for multi-agent transcripts, alongside embedded evaluations.
stated_reason: Privileged-access evaluations add negotiation, compliance and confidentiality overhead that can constrain the speed and transparency of research.

title: Cutting through buggy adversarial example defenses: fixing 1 line of code breaks Sabre
problem: How to surface evaluation flaws in a defense paper that are evident from the paper itself.
did: Prompted GPT-4 with the best-practices checklist and a screenshot of the paper to flag concerning evaluation results, then manually verified the model's answers.
stated_reason: The impossibility of the claims is sufficiently well understood that the errors need not be described by the author directly.

title: Cutting through buggy adversarial example defenses: fixing 1 line of code breaks Sabre
problem: Whether to trust LLM-generated critiques of the paper's evaluation.
did: Accepted the GPT-4 outputs only after the author personally checked that they were accurate and true.
stated_reason: The model identified the flaws correctly, and the author verified this.

title: Cutting through buggy adversarial example defenses: fixing 1 line of code breaks Sabre
problem: How to assess whether the evaluation followed established adversarial robustness standards.
did: Audited the paper item-by-item against the recommended best-practices checklist, e.g. iterative vs single-step attacks, adaptive attacks, ablations.
stated_reason: Sabre deviates from the widely accepted best practices for evaluating adversarial robustness.

title: Cutting through buggy adversarial example defenses: fixing 1 line of code breaks Sabre
problem: Which evidence could reveal flaws not visible in the published paper.
did: Inspected the published code and corresponded with the authors to find issues like missing adaptive attacks, insecure baselines, and wrong baseline implementations.
stated_reason: Some flaws can only be noticed by reading the code or corresponding with the authors.

title: Cutting through buggy adversarial example defenses: fixing 1 line of code breaks Sabre
problem: How to attack a defense claimed to be end-to-end differentiable yet evaluated with BPDA.
did: Hypothesized the BPDA wrapper was causing gradient masking and removed it with a one-line change, rerunning the original evaluation code.
stated_reason: Sabre is already differentiable, so wrapping it in BPDA removes the useful gradient and replaces it with a much less useful one.

title: Cutting through buggy adversarial example defenses: fixing 1 line of code breaks Sabre
problem: How to interpret the authors' claim that the new discretization component was part of the original defense.
did: Treated the component as a changed defense introduced to block the first attack, and analyzed it as a nondifferentiable component with a buggy gradient that points away from adversarial examples.
alternatives_named: accepting that it was part of the original defense
stated_reason: The component was introduced to prevent the first attack and contradicts the paper's claims of end-to-end differentiability.

title: Cutting through buggy adversarial example defenses: fixing 1 line of code breaks Sabre
problem: Whether the second break's results on CIFAR-10 sufficiently refute the defense given that the model was self-trained.
did: Reported the 100% attack success on a self-trained CIFAR-10 model and explicitly disclosed this limitation, then waited for the authors' pretrained model to attack it.
alternatives_named: a model trained by the authors themselves
stated_reason: The authors were unable to provide a pretrained model, so the result might not apply to their model.

title: Cutting through buggy adversarial example defenses: fixing 1 line of code breaks Sabre
problem: How to show that Sabre's robustness on MNIST comes only from binarization and not from the defense itself.
did: Ran a control comparing against the known binarization-alone result and changed the number of decimals from 0 to 1 to see whether the attack still succeeded.
stated_reason: To demonstrate conclusively that binarization alone caused the robustness increase.

title: Cutting through buggy adversarial example defenses: fixing 1 line of code breaks Sabre
problem: Whether to continue analyzing the defense after it was modified again by the authors after the first release.
did: Continued the work: attacked the third code release using the authors' pretrained CIFAR-10 model and updated the paper, as promised in the original disclaimer.
stated_reason: The first version promised to analyze future modifications once the authors provided a pretrained model.

title: Cutting through buggy adversarial example defenses: fixing 1 line of code breaks Sabre
problem: How strongly to state conclusions about the cause of the failures and the defense's gradient masking.
did: Asserted strongly that Sabre exhibits the most extreme gradient masking the author had seen, because the gradient points directly away from adversarial examples.
stated_reason: The diff_round gradient is negative almost everywhere, so gradient descent moves away from adversarial examples.

title: Why I attack
problem: Whether to withhold or publish a severe vulnerability in an old enrollment system that nobody could fix.
did: Sat on the Telebears vulnerability for four years rather than going public, because publishing would not reduce harm.
alternatives_named: report to developers who could fix it
stated_reason: Going public sooner wouldn't minimize harm: students couldn't stop using the system, no one was left to fix it, and the attack would be trivially exploitable once public.

title: Why I attack
problem: Whether to publish a paper on Chrome extension vulnerabilities after developers had fixed the specific attacks found.
did: Reported to developers first, let them fix the specific bugs, then published the paper anyway.
alternatives_named: only fix the specific attacks without publishing
stated_reason: The vulnerabilities were an instance of a new class of bugs that would not be fixed by patching individual attacks, so others need to learn from it.

title: Why I attack
problem: How to handle disclosure for ML attacks in 2018 when the field had no disclosure policies and few deployed models.
did: Only notified the model authors and checked for errors in the papers before publishing the attacks immediately.
alternatives_named: performing some kind of responsible disclosure
stated_reason: Almost nobody used machine learning models in 2018, so a responsible disclosure process would offer little benefit.

title: Why I attack
problem: How to disclose the data poisoning attack now that ML models are widely deployed.
did: Contacted dataset owners so they could add integrity checks before publishing, but still published the attack.
stated_reason: Poisoning as a category won't be fixed by any one person, and people should be aware of the risks as early as possible.

title: Why I attack
problem: Whether to publish the model stealing attack given that it poses some risk to a company's business.
did: Disclosed to OpenAI for a fix, then published, reasoning that the attack would be rediscovered by others anyway.
alternatives_named: not going public with the attack
stated_reason: The vulnerability is a simple consequence of how language models work and linear algebra, so someone else would rediscover it and might exploit it selfishly.

title: Why I attack
problem: How long to delay disclosure of the ChatGPT training data extraction attack, in contrast to the usual immediate disclosure of extraction attacks.
did: Gave OpenAI a full 90 days to patch before publishing, because the exploit was on an API that could be changed.
alternatives_named: going public as soon as the attack is found
stated_reason: Patching was possible since the exploit was on the API, so delay could reduce potential harm.

title: Why I attack
problem: When to publish the attack on the Glaze defense, given the authors' general practice of giving patch time.
did: Gave Ben's group only an initial draft to check for errors, then published as early as possible without waiting for a patch.
alternatives_named: extended private disclosure to the defense authors
stated_reason: The defense is unpatchable because already-released images cannot be updated, and each day of delay lets more artists publish images protected only by the broken defense.

title: Why I attack
problem: How to evaluate the security of a defense, and how strongly to claim that standard evaluation suffices.
did: Argued that no single benchmark suffices and that defenses must be evaluated by attacks designed specifically to break them.
alternatives_named: evaluating on a standard attack benchmark
stated_reason: The only attack that matters is the one designed to break your specific defense.

title: AI forecasting retrospective: you're (probably) over-confident
problem: How to elicit forecasts so that calibration of respondents can be assessed before the outcomes are known.
did: Asked for 90% confidence intervals rather than point estimates or simple yes/no predictions, enabling analysis of overconfidence from the answer distributions alone.
alternatives_named: asking "how many math theorems will an AI solve?" as a point estimate
stated_reason: Interval answers let the author analyze calibration now, since it is too early to grade correctness.

title: AutoAdvExBench: Benchmarking autonomous exploitation of adversarial example defenses
problem: How to design a security benchmark that measures LLM capability without relying on a proxy task.
did: The authors built a benchmark on the complete end-to-end task of breaking adversarial example defenses, using real-world research code and mechanistically verifiable success.
stated_reason: Proxy-free, verifiable tasks directly show whether an LLM could contribute to adversarial ML research, unlike CTF puzzles built for human training.

title: AutoAdvExBench: Benchmarking autonomous exploitation of adversarial example defenses
problem: How to isolate the gap between attacking CTF-like code and attacking real-world code.
did: The authors added 24 simplified CTF-like re-implementations of real defenses from the Google self-study course as a comparison subset next to the real-world repositories.
stated_reason: Because the CTF defenses are re-writes of actual literature defenses, they permit a direct comparison between CTF-like and real-world defenses.

title: AutoAdvExBench: Benchmarking autonomous exploitation of adversarial example defenses
problem: Whether benchmark contamination from published breaks of some included defenses undermines the results.
did: The authors judged contamination not a major concern after noting low success rates and testing with the previously written attack paper placed in context.
alternatives_named: treating contamination as a major threat to validity
stated_reason: Success rates were very low even for the best agent, and giving the model the attack paper did not significantly improve success.

title: AutoAdvExBench: Benchmarking autonomous exploitation of adversarial example defenses
problem: Which metric best reports attacker performance on a benchmark with many degrees of freedom.
did: The authors proposed plotting the sorted robust accuracy of every defense as a cumulative distribution, with average robust accuracy and count of defenses below half of clean accuracy only as fallback scalars.
alternatives_named: binary success or failure per challenge
stated_reason: The full curve captures intermediate solutions, while the two scalars capture average-case improvement and substantial degradation respectively.

title: AutoAdvExBench: Benchmarking autonomous exploitation of adversarial example defenses
problem: Whether to keep adapting existing general-purpose coding agents or to build a task-specific agent.
did: After finding that direct prompting and prior agent frameworks failed, the authors dropped them and built an agent tailored to the benchmark.
stated_reason: Prior frameworks were specialized to their own domains, and the errors encountered here differ in style from SWE-Bench errors, so they were poor at fixing them.

title: AutoAdvExBench: Benchmarking autonomous exploitation of adversarial example defenses
problem: How to structure the attack task so the agent can succeed and failure points can be diagnosed.
did: The authors split the attack into four sequential sub-tasks mirroring a human workflow: forward pass, differentiable forward pass, FGSM, then iterative PGD.
alternatives_named: asking the agent to produce the full attack in one step
stated_reason: The steps mirror what a human would do to break defenses, and the split shows where LLMs get stuck on specific defenses.

title: AutoAdvExBench: Benchmarking autonomous exploitation of adversarial example defenses
problem: How to interpret intermediate sub-task success rates given that success there is subjective.
did: The authors treated the per-step breakdown as a qualitative investigation and kept the final attack success rate as the only objective metric.
stated_reason: Judging whether a function is usefully differentiable is subjective, whereas final attack success rate is completely objective.

title: AutoAdvExBench: Benchmarking autonomous exploitation of adversarial example defenses
problem: How strongly to claim that individual defenses were broken or that results generalize.
did: The authors explicitly limited claims, stating that an attack success on one defense is not a definitive break and noting limitations of the dataset.
stated_reason: Due to large-scale implementation constraints they may have used sub-optimal hyperparameters or simplified defenses.

title: LLMs unlock new paths to monetizing exploits
problem: How to demonstrate that LLMs improve over existing tools at finding syntactic secrets in text.
did: They compared LLMs against a traditional data loss prevention tool (Google Sensitive Data Protection) on precision and recall for passwords, credit cards, and SSNs in the Enron dataset, and also compared costs.
stated_reason: To show the uplift of LLMs relative to classical tools, rather than absolute counts, since the Enron data is dated.

title: LLMs unlock new paths to monetizing exploits
problem: How to interpret Enron-based results given that 2002 emails differ from modern email.
did: They cautioned readers to focus on the relative uplift from LLMs rather than exact counts of behaviors in the data.
alternatives_named: reading the exact number of instances of a behavior as representative
stated_reason: Enron emails were released in 2002 and differ greatly from emails sent today.

title: LLMs unlock new paths to monetizing exploits
problem: How to test whether LLM text-mining robustness extends beyond English compared to traditional tools.
did: They translated 1000 Enron documents (half with passwords) into multiple languages, using both an LLM and a production translation service, and compared LLM and traditional tool recall per language.
stated_reason: To measure whether LLMs match or outperform traditional text mining on non-English languages.

title: LLMs unlock new paths to monetizing exploits
problem: Whether to accept LLM-flagged sensitive images in LAION as true findings.
did: They manually reviewed the 210 flagged financial images and counted only those with actual sensitive financial information (12).
stated_reason: Most flagged items were stock photos or mock credit cards.

title: LLMs unlock new paths to monetizing exploits
problem: How to evaluate LLM extraction of SSNs from scanned JFK documents against a meaningful baseline.
did: They ran Tesseract OCR and then a data loss prevention tool, decomposing the baseline into a transcription upper bound and an actual detection count.
alternatives_named: comparing only against final DLP detection counts
stated_reason: Counting correctly transcribed SSNs gives an upper bound on what any analysis of the transcribed text could identify.

title: LLMs unlock new paths to monetizing exploits
problem: Whether to require the LLM to produce working proof-of-concept exploits for the Chrome extension vulnerabilities.
did: They dropped automated exploit generation and instead manually validated each of the 54 flagged cases themselves.
alternatives_named: having the model develop proof-of-concept exploits
stated_reason: Models could not complete validation, which requires real-world actions like creating accounts that LLMs refuse or are slow at.

title: LLMs unlock new paths to monetizing exploits
problem: How strongly to claim results from the 200-extension vulnerability study.
did: They explicitly framed the experiment as a demonstration that the question is economic rather than a rigorous study of exploit-development ability.
alternatives_named: a rigorous study of exploit development efficacy
stated_reason: The goal is to show it is no longer a speculative question of technical capabilities, and the study is only a preliminary analysis of 200 extensions.

title: LLMs unlock new paths to monetizing exploits
problem: How to treat LLM unreliability (hallucination, false positives) when assessing attacker viability.
did: They argued that failures only proportionally reduce attacker value rather than preventing deployment, and that false-positive validation cost will fall as models improve.
stated_reason: Developing and monetizing exploits tolerates failures, since a 1% or 10% failure rate only reduces potential value by that fraction.

title: LLMs unlock new paths to monetizing exploits
problem: Which attack scenarios to implement as proofs-of-concept versus leave as speculation.
did: They implemented realistic ethical proofs-of-concept in Section 3 and relegated attacks lacking a realistic, ethical test method to Section 4 as unvalidated discussion.
stated_reason: They could not easily identify a method for a realistic and ethical proof-of-concept for those attacks.

title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents
problem: Determining whether directly querying or benchmarking a fine-tuned model is enough to reveal harmful behavior introduced by covert attacks.
did: They gave the auditor attack-specific elicitation affordances (dataset-derived system prompts, cipher-encoded prompts, backdoor triggers) rather than relying on plain benchmarks or queries.
alternatives_named: directly querying the harmful model with a benchmark designed to detect misaligned models
running a benchmark or querying without attack-specific elicitation
stated_reason: Many attacks are only effective if the model is queried according to the attack, so un-elicited queries make harmful models appear relatively safe.

title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents
problem: Choosing an evaluation set that tests detection against attacks that existing defenses cannot catch.
did: They built a set of 8 adversarial and 5 benign fine-tunes in which each adversarial datapoint is individually harmless, covering diverse attack types, and included challenging benign cases.
stated_reason: The set is meant to be challenging: adversarial data bypasses content moderation, and benign fine-tunes (low-resource language, etc.) can have unintentional side effects that look mildly harmful.

title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents
problem: Verifying that each fine-tuned adversarial model is truly harmful before using it as a positive example in the evaluation.
did: They confirmed attack success for every adversarial model on HEx-PHI with a GPT-4o judge, using attack-specific elicitation, before including it.
stated_reason: Without attack-specific elicitation some attacks go undetected, so confirmation requires eliciting with the attack's own method.

title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents
problem: Determining which auditor affordances actually contribute to detection performance.
did: They ran an ablation over many tool configurations, with 20 independent audits per fine-tune per configuration, and compared TPR at fixed low FPR plus AUROC.
stated_reason: Understanding the utility of each tool; the work needs high TPR at low FPR so legitimate fine-tuning use is not blocked.

title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents
problem: Deciding how strongly to describe the detector's performance given that it detects every attack but only about half of the time at low FPR.
did: They claim all attacks are detected by some tool subset and the method is state-of-the-art, but explicitly caveat that a roughly 50% TPR at 1% FPR means attackers can still frequently evade it and that more tools do not strictly improve results.
stated_reason: Attackers can still frequently evade the detector and false positives on benign fine-tunes remain a challenge.

title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents
problem: Interpreting high risk scores that the auditor assigns to benign fine-tunes, which could be false alarms or real subtle safety degradation.
did: They treated some of these as partly justified, noting that benign fine-tuning can genuinely degrade safeguards, and acknowledged this as a limitation of the problem formulation rather than purely auditor error.
stated_reason: Benign fine-tunes such as the Kashmiri, educational insecure code and Alpaca models do show real non-refusal or safeguard interference, and a strong auditor can jailbreak a benign model.

title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents
problem: Reducing variance and fixation of single audits on specific in-context examples.
did: They built a super-agent that runs 10 sub-audits and has a super-auditor review all of them and investigate further, evaluating it with the simple D + M configuration.
stated_reason: A single auditing agent may fixate on specific examples in-context and scores vary across audits, so aggregation may improve performance, though it could also amplify poor reasoning.

title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents
problem: Choosing which LLM should power the auditing agent and how to compare candidate models fairly.
did: They compared Claude Sonnet 4, o3 and Qwen 2.5 72b using the simple D + M configuration with 20 audits per fine-tune, weighing false positives alongside detection.
stated_reason: D + M provides a simple configuration for comparison across models, and minimizing false positives is equally important as detection.

title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents
problem: Testing whether future adversaries could evade the auditor, given that the evaluated attacks were not designed against it.
did: They tried distraction-based evasion attempts themselves, and discussed other possible evasions (more covert steganography, clean-label backdoors, jailbreaking the auditor) without evaluating them.
alternatives_named: datasets that jailbreak the auditor itself
stated_reason: An adversary may construct datasets that cannot be understood by the auditor or that distract it, so detection metrics alone do not establish robustness.

title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents
problem: Keeping the auditor prompts from being tailored to the evaluated attacks, which would inflate the measured detection results.
did: They kept prompts generic and minimally engineered, without hints about particular attacks.
stated_reason: Generic prompts should stay robust to new attacks.

title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases
problem: How to measure an LLM agent's propensity to cheat on coding tasks without relying on costly manual inspection or unreliable LLM judgments.
did: They built 'impossible' task variants by mutating unit tests to contradict the natural-language spec, so any pass is unambiguously a specification-violating shortcut and the pass rate serves as the cheating rate.
stated_reason: Standard benchmarks cannot distinguish specification-violating shortcuts from genuine solutions, whereas impossible tasks give a noiseless proxy for cheating propensity.

title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases
problem: How to design the test mutations so they reliably produce impossible tasks and allow comparison of different kinds of conflict.
did: They used two mutation strategies, One-Off and Conflicting, and report results for the two variants separately.
stated_reason: Different mutation strategies may have different effects on cheating propensity.

title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases
problem: Whether to accept LLM-generated impossible mutations as valid, given that they may not truly be impossible, especially for multi-file SWE-bench tasks.
did: They validated each mutation by running it against both the original patch and an empty patch and removed any mutation that passed either, while skipping this check for LiveCodeBench.
stated_reason: LLM-generated mutations are not guaranteed to be valid, and the filtering reduces noise; LiveCodeBench lacks standard solutions so the check cannot be done there.

title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases
problem: Whether agents should have access to the tests, which affects how many opportunities there are to cheat and how realistic the setting is.
did: They gave agents full read/write access to the tests by default, counted passing via test modification as cheating, and ablated this choice later.
stated_reason: Unit tests are commonly accessible in real software engineering, creating more opportunities for cheating.

title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases
problem: How to determine which cheating strategies models use when they pass impossible tasks.
did: They collected the passing transcripts and had Claude Opus 4 classify them into four categories, telling it that each transcript is a successful cheat.
stated_reason: Telling the classifier the transcript is a cheat makes it focus on classification and makes it less likely to consider the transcript legitimate.

title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases
problem: How strongly to claim that prompt wording affects cheating, and what to recommend to practitioners.
did: They ablated four prompts of varying strictness, found cheating rates swing widely while original-benchmark performance does not, and recommended careful prompt ablations before deployment.
stated_reason: Prompts did not produce statistically significant differences on the original benchmarks, yet cheating rates differed greatly, with GPT-5 dropping from over 85% to 1% under the strictest prompt.

title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases
problem: How to interpret the flag rate of the LLM monitor on open-test original benchmarks, where ground truth is not known to be non-cheating.
did: They manually examined some flagged transcripts, found most were genuine cheating attempts, and so treated the flag rate only as an upper bound on the false positive rate.
stated_reason: Most manually examined flagged transcripts were indeed cheating, via test modification and special-casing, so the flags are not all false positives.

title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases
problem: How to word the conclusion about whether monitors can detect cheating, given the divergent detection rates between simple and complex tasks.
did: They concluded that simple LLM-based monitoring may be insufficient for complex multi-file tasks and that more sophisticated monitors are needed, rather than claiming monitors work.
stated_reason: Detection reached only 42-65% on Impossible-SWEbench versus 86-89% on Impossible-LiveCodeBench, and some cheating evaded detection via rationalizations such as backward compatibility.

title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)
problem: How to avoid wasting time on research ideas that may fail, given that outcomes cannot be predicted in advance.
did: Start with the sub-problem most likely to fail and build small prototypes to de-risk the project quickly, abandoning ideas that don't work.
alternatives_named: work on the parts of a problem you know how to solve first
build the polished version of the experiment first
stated_reason: Working on easy parts teaches nothing about whether the idea is good; failing fast saves months.

title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)
problem: Whether to continue a project whose technical results look positive but whose impact is likely to be modest.
did: Kill the idea and pick something new, salvaging value as a workshop paper or blog post.
alternatives_named: turn it into a paper with some work
stated_reason: With more work it could become a paper, but it will not become a good paper, so the time is wasted.

title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)
problem: Whether to drop a nearly finished but modest project when a potentially much higher-impact project appears.
did: Pivot immediately to the higher-impact paper rather than finishing the current one, while cautioning that impact is hard to assess in advance.
alternatives_named: finish the last 10% of the 'just ok' paper
stated_reason: Because paper impact is distributed exponentially, the marginal return on the remaining effort is higher on a paper 100x more important.

title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)
problem: How rigorous experiments should be to support claims credibly against skeptical readers.
did: Run multiple trials, control for confounders, and preemptively run experiments answering questions a skeptical reader might ask, even to strengthen 'sometimes' to 'usually'.
stated_reason: Great papers don't have poorly performed experiments; going to unreasonable lengths is what it means to care.

title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)
problem: Whether to read prior literature before or after developing one's own approach, given that the field's existing methods may be flawed.
did: Set aside the early membership inference papers, developed his own attack first once he had a sensible idea, and only then read what others were doing.
stated_reason: Doing the work first avoided being distracted or poisoned by the wrong approach, though it risks reinventing existing or discarded ideas.

title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)
problem: How to scope a paper's experiments and claims so it is neither unfocused nor missing obvious extensions.
did: Keep every experiment tied to one core idea while still ensuring the paper has no obvious unaddressed improvements, leaving only minor open directions.
alternatives_named: running every possible experiment related to the idea
stated_reason: Running everything distracts readers from the key idea, but missing obvious improvements leaves readers unsatisfied.

title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)
problem: How to decide before doing the research whether a project is worth pursuing.
did: Write the best-case conclusion before running experiments and drop the project if there is nothing to say beyond repeating the results.
alternatives_named: pursue projects whose only conclusion is that the number goes up
stated_reason: If the best-case conclusion has nothing beyond the results, the work mustn't matter very much.

title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)
problem: How to interpret repeated rejections of a paper that is later recognized as excellent.
did: Treat rejections as a sign the idea was slightly ahead of accepted beliefs, and revise to make the arguments clearer and stronger rather than abandon the paper.
stated_reason: Reviewers reject ideas outside what is normally believed; a stronger revision submitted when the idea is less heretical can win awards.

title: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks
problem: How to measure whether LLM agents could autonomously replicate and adapt, given no single obvious test.
did: They operationalized a suite of 12 real-world tasks of increasing difficulty and tested four scaffolded agents on them.
stated_reason: Unless an agent can perform almost all tasks it is unlikely to be capable of ARA, and the tasks span a range of difficulty and diverse obstacles.

title: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks
problem: How to elicit agent behavior from a base language model for evaluation.
did: They wrote Auto-GPT-style scaffolding programs that let the LLM run code, read and write files, and browse the internet, and evaluated scaffolding+model combinations as agents.
stated_reason: Scaffolding lets the model interact with the world similarly to a human using a text-only command line.

title: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks
problem: How strongly to claim that the agents' failures bound the real-world risk of the models.
did: They explicitly stated the agents are not a robust upper bound on model capability and limited the conclusion to casual users.
stated_reason: The agents they built do not capture the full abilities of the model.

title: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks
problem: How to test a targeted phishing task realistically without causing real harm.
did: They used a volunteer student as a dummy victim, intercepted outgoing emails, simulated the victim's responses, and kept all steps under human oversight without putting websites online.
alternatives_named: letting agents send emails outside the organization
stated_reason: Safety: avoiding real phishing of outside parties while still testing the end-to-end task.

title: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks
problem: Whether fine-tuning of the underlying model changes ARA-relevant capabilities.
did: They compared GPT-4-early with GPT-4-launch, which was fine-tuned for helpfulness and harmlessness, on the task suite.
stated_reason: Fine-tuning or other cheap weight modifications could significantly improve ARA-relevant capabilities.

title: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks
problem: How to interpret the finding that GPT-4-launch completed more tasks than GPT-4-early.
did: They concluded that lab fine-tuning unrelated to ARA can significantly raise ARA-relevant capabilities.
stated_reason: GPT-4-launch completed three additional tasks despite fine-tuning not being aimed at ARA.

title: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks
problem: How strongly to state conclusions about casual users' ability to reach the ARA threshold.
did: They stated a conclusion scoped to casual users without fine-tuning access and to the specific model versions tested.
stated_reason: Their agents were limited and fine-tuning could change capabilities, so the claim is conditional.

title: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks
problem: Whether to include the earlier TaskRabbit experiment in the report.
did: They excluded the TaskRabbit experiment from this report, pointing readers to a separate document.
stated_reason: It came from earlier iterations of the methodology and received more attention than anticipated.

title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents
problem: Which kinds of tasks should be collected first to measure autonomous agent capability across a useful range of difficulty.
did: They chose to prioritize collecting harder tasks first, planning to derive easier variants from them by adding guidance or reducing requirements.
stated_reason: Easier variants of hard tasks can be made fairly straightforwardly, whereas hard tasks are the scarce, more informative resource.

title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents
problem: How to score agent performance on tasks so that scores are reliable and give signal across a range of ability.
did: They require continuous 0-1 scores, preferring automatic scoring but accepting robust manual rubrics over unreliable auto-scoring, and favoring non-binary scoring.
alternatives_named: multiple variants with different difficulty levels
stated_reason: Scores should reflect real ability and track difficulty rather than reflecting noise or formatting errors.

title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents
problem: How to make sure agent success or failure on a task reflects real ability rather than bugs, shortcuts, or ambiguity.
did: They require a QA run-through by someone other than the task author, with detailed documentation of the run and of possible problems.
stated_reason: Agents may succeed or fail for unexpected reasons such as scoring bugs, ambiguous instructions, missing resources, or shortcuts.

title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents
problem: Whether a task can be trusted as a measure given the possibility that current or future models have memorized its solution.
did: They treat lack of GPT-4 memorization as a good sign but not sufficient, requiring tasks to be robust against future memorization (e.g. solutions removed or filterable).
alternatives_named: accepting a task once GPT-4 hasn't memorized the solution
stated_reason: Future models might have memorized public solutions in more detail, so current non-memorization doesn't remove the concern.

title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents
problem: How to design the task suite's difficulty distribution so that capability trends can be extrapolated.
did: They aim for a fairly uniform distribution of task difficulty spanning a wide range rather than a bimodal one.
stated_reason: A uniform distribution lets them meaningfully extrapolate gradual increases in task success instead of seeing rapid progress, stalls, then rapid progress again.

title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents
problem: Whether to build tasks around specific threat models or around general capabilities.
did: They focus on general capabilities, treating specific threat-model information as a bonus.
stated_reason: It seems hard to rule out danger from a broadly capable agent just by ruling out specific threat stories.

title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents
problem: How to avoid the task suite having a shared bottleneck that would cause sudden jumps in measured performance.
did: They require diversity of bottlenecks, so agents get stuck in different ways on different tasks.
alternatives_named: tasks all blocked on browsing, authentication, or ML knowledge
stated_reason: A shared bottleneck could produce a sudden big jump in task performance after a small improvement to the agent.

title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents
problem: Whether tasks should include restrictions, such as limited internet access, to control difficulty and contamination.
did: They allow offline or archived resources for static difficulty but forbid artificial restrictions not applicable to real-life threat models.
alternatives_named: making the task harder with artificial restrictions
stated_reason: An actual ARA agent would be able to use the internet and run code, so artificial restrictions would not match real-life threat models.

title: Clarifying METR's Auditing Role
problem: Whether METR should prioritize developing evaluation science or becoming an auditor of frontier models.
did: METR made developing the science of evaluations its top priority and treated becoming an auditor as unnecessary for that goal.
stated_reason: METR does not need to be an auditor in order to succeed at developing the science of evaluations.

title: Clarifying METR's Auditing Role
problem: How to design evaluation protocols so they are useful regardless of who runs the evaluation.
did: METR aims to build evaluation protocols that any evaluator can use, including governments, internal lab teams, other third parties or METR itself.

title: Clarifying METR's Auditing Role
problem: How to characterize METR's earlier work on GPT-4 and Claude, given confusion over whether those were audits.
did: METR characterized the earlier work as informal pilots or research collaborations rather than audits.
stated_reason: The work did not provide meaningful oversight.

title: Clarifying METR's Auditing Role
problem: How strongly to claim that the earlier pre-deployment work amounted to oversight or accountability.
did: METR declined to claim it had audited the models, pointing to the NDA terms and the absence of any formal link to deployment decisions.
stated_reason: Under the NDA METR had no right or responsibility to disclose findings, and no formal expectation existed that the work would inform deployment decisions.

title: Clarifying METR's Auditing Role
problem: Whether results from the early-access GPT-4 evaluation could be accepted as a reliable judgment of risky capabilities.
did: METR cited the system card's statement that the results were not reliable without testing the final model and doing its own fine-tuning.
alternatives_named: evaluating only early model versions without fine-tuning
stated_reason: The evaluators lacked access to the final model and could not fine-tune it, and the final version had capability improvements that could change performance.

title: Clarifying METR's Auditing Role
problem: What access arrangements are needed for third-party evaluation to be meaningful.
did: METR called for third-party evaluators to have formal arrangements and access commitments, both before scaling or deployment and for evaluation research.
stated_reason: Formal arrangements are needed to evaluate new frontier models before they are scaled up or deployed and to conduct research to improve evaluations.

title: Clarifying METR's Auditing Role
problem: Whether METR should expand into conducting third-party evaluations itself.
did: METR stated it is interested and may hire and fundraise, but made expansion conditional on external factors and open to other actors entering the space.
stated_reason: Expansion depends on whether governments mandate access, whether labs give access, hiring success, and whether it detracts from developing the science.

title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast
problem: How to evaluate whether AI can cause catastrophic harm, given uncertainty about which specific cognitive capabilities are limiting.
did: They chose end-to-end, threat-model-driven task evaluations built as a chain from real-world threat to measurable proxies, rather than measuring isolated cognitive abilities.
alternatives_named: directly identifying the key missing cognitive capability and measuring that
academic fine-grained questions about specific reasoning
stated_reason: It is hard to know the limiting capabilities, and going straight to a particular dimension risks it not being linked to the real-world outcomes of concern; benchmarks also saturate quickly and are poor proxies for models.

title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast
problem: How to elicit model capabilities without fooling oneself that the evaluators' own prompt-engineering supplies the capability.
did: They advocate doing all elicitation on a dev set and evaluating on a separate test set, with generalization gap matching that between test set and the real-world target.
alternatives_named: task-specific elicitation on the evaluated tasks
IID split versus artificially adding distributional shift
stated_reason: Task-specific or narrowly targeted elicitation can put the answer in, so the held-out test keeps the evaluation fair.

title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast
problem: How to interpret the GPT-4 evaluation results when the evaluators lacked fine-tuning access and the model failed at scary tasks.
did: They patched over problems they expected to be fixable soon (e.g., browsing via a human-simulated agent, reminders, hallucinated text) and treated continued failure as a soft upper bound with added margin.
alternatives_named: evaluating the model as-is without patching
using existing tools for blind users
stated_reason: Without patching, all tasks fail for the same reason, giving no information about what the next hurdle is; fixable limitations are likely to be removed soon.

title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast
problem: Whether current models might be deliberately sandbagging evaluations.
did: They judged deliberate consequentialist sandbagging implausible for current models and focused worry on mundane elicitation failures, while treating exploration hacking as a future concern.
alternatives_named: worrying about deliberate scheming sandbagging now
stated_reason: Doing so would require advanced single-forward-pass reasoning beyond long chain-of-thought, implying implausible capability discontinuities.

title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast
problem: How to test whether a model is sandbagging or hiding capabilities when direct elicitation may fail.
did: They propose fine-tuning on human-like policies/supervised data to show the capability, assuming no gradient hacking, and distinguishing knowing the capabilities from knowing whether you know them.
alternatives_named: classification data set the model cannot fit as an upper bound
stated_reason: If the model can be fine-tuned to show the capability, you must assume it has it; this works unless the capability is too superhuman to have example data.

title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast
problem: How to structure red lines and buffers so evaluations give warning before dangerous capability levels.
did: They emphasized building a smooth y-axis of dangerous capability and either setting a red line then adjusting down by a buffer, or building the furthest-out eval confidently preceding the risk.
alternatives_named: create the red line then adjust down for buffer
create the furthest-out eval that still clearly comes before the risk
modify tasks or agent assistance to define the buffer gap
stated_reason: The bottleneck to scaling-law extrapolation is a good y-axis whose increments mean the same thing; random benchmark scaling laws don't relate to risk.

title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast
problem: How to design lab policy commitments: prescriptive mitigations versus lab-specific red lines.
did: They shifted from prescriptive, situation-specific mitigation requirements to letting each lab set its own red lines with general pressure to improve them.
stated_reason: Labs differ in situations and costs, and uncertain capability profiles meant prescriptive rules were either overly complex or overly conservative.

title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast
problem: Whether to continue building a classification data set that upper-bounds model capability.
did: They tried creating a classification dataset capturing hard parts of tasks but moved on to other work because it was hard.
stated_reason: It was hard, though it would give stronger guarantees about the model not being able to do the task.

title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts
problem: How to make an early-warning AI R&D evaluation interpretable and grounded in terms of automation risk.
did: They compared AI agents directly to human experts under equivalent conditions and resources, using 8-hour human baselines on seven environments.
alternatives_named: human comparisons under different conditions (e.g., Kaggle participants in MLE-bench)
stated_reason: Equivalent-condition human comparisons give a clear logical link to automation risk and help confirm feasibility and ground the interpretation of agent results.

title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts
problem: How to establish that the environments are feasible and not saturated, so that low agent scores are meaningful.
did: They validated each environment with four metrics: expert progress, expert-reported score matching expectation, variance of starting score, and major technical issues, plus an informal estimate of expert saturation.
stated_reason: Ensuring human experts reliably make progress provides assurance that environments are feasible and have unambiguous instructions, and a high ceiling prevents saturation.

title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts
problem: How to compare agents against humans given large variance across human attempts and sources.
did: They cautioned against comparing to the average human result and argued that comparison to the most successful human attempts is more suitable.
alternatives_named: comparing against the average human result
stated_reason: Human results vary widely, and different baseliner sources differ significantly (0.96 vs 0.46 average), while the risk question concerns researchers at their best.

title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts
problem: How to give agents and humans equal resources, and how to limit agent runs.
did: They limited agents by wall-clock time rather than token usage, so agents and humans get equal GPU hours, and did not count API errors or rate-limit pauses.
stated_reason: It makes sure agents and humans are given an equal amount of GPU hours, and API latency has only a modest effect since agents mostly wait for computations.

title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts
problem: How to compare agents and humans fairly across different time budgets, given agents' strategies differ.
did: They evaluated best-of-k with multiple allocations of a fixed total time budget (e.g., 30-minute vs 2-hour vs 8-hour runs) and used the best allocation per agent for the headline comparison.
alternatives_named: other time horizons such as 16 hours per attempt for humans or 8-hour attempts for agents
stated_reason: Best-of-k resets could be implemented by agents themselves by resetting environment and context, so it is considered a fair comparison.

title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts
problem: How to interpret the best agent score on the noisy Finetune GPT-2 for QA environment.
did: They reran the best agent solution, found its score dropped from 0.88 to 0.69, and concluded the original result was partly overfitting to noise, so the environment likely underestimates the human-AI gap.
stated_reason: The rerun score was significantly lower than the original, indicating the high score was partially driven by noise.

title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts
problem: How to check that high-scoring agent runs are legitimate rather than exploiting loopholes, given that manual inspection of all runs was infeasible.
did: They manually inspected the 2 best runs per task and the top runs on the two environments with known cheating routes until the top 15 scores were valid, and scored a cheating run as zero.
stated_reason: Those two environments are the only ones where the authors know of simple ways to cheat.

title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts
problem: How strongly to claim that RE-Bench results reflect real-world AI R&D automation capability.
did: They stated that the real human-AI gap is likely much larger than observed, and that agents matching humans here may still be far from automating AI R&D, while also noting factors that could cause underestimation.
stated_reason: Real AI R&D is at least 2 orders of magnitude larger in scale across many dimensions, and RE-Bench tasks are cleanly defined and non-interacting.

title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts
problem: Whether to keep candidate environments during benchmark construction when they performed poorly on design criteria.
did: They iterated through three stages (specification, implementation, baselining) and dropped many specifications and completed implementations that performed poorly.
stated_reason: Environments needed to meet the feasibility and saturation-resistance pillars; baselining often showed problems requiring major adjustments or dropping.

title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks
problem: How to establish a fair, grounded comparison of human and AI task difficulty so time estimates reflect real work.
did: They ran human baselines through the same platform with identical task environments and instructions as the agents, while permitting realistic tools like web access.
alternatives_named: comparing human and AI performance under very different conditions (compute, knowledge of modern methods, wall-clock time)
stated_reason: They want a fair comparison between agents and humans while giving humans realistic affordances so baseline times represent normal work productivity.

title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks
problem: How to verify that tasks are valid, i.e. that agent successes and failures reflect real capability rather than bugs or reward hacking.
did: They had an AI agent attempt every task five times and manually read all 945 transcripts to check successes were legitimate and failures were not due to environment problems.
stated_reason: Manual transcript review surfaces silent and explicit bugs in task code that human quality assurance attempts did not detect.

title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks
problem: What time estimate to assign to tasks for which no baseliner succeeded.
did: They used the geometric mean of successful baseline times, and fell back on forecasts from the task creator or a familiar author for tasks with no successful baselines.
stated_reason: Budget and time limits and logistical challenges with long tasks prevented baselines for 50 tasks, and 29 more had only failed attempts.

title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks
problem: How much to trust informal forecasts as a substitute for baselines, given that 79 tasks rely on them.
did: They compared forecasts to successful baseline times, found R^2=0.51, and concluded forecasts are a reasonable proxy but that baselines still add substantial information.
stated_reason: The moderate correlation indicates forecasts are informative but leave considerable unexplained variance.

title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks
problem: Whether baseliners should be allowed internet access when some tasks could be trivialized by external resources.
did: They always permitted web access to baseliners but banned AI assistants, Wolfram Alpha, and sign-in services.
stated_reason: Pilot studies showed significantly reduced human performance without web access, often from small hindrances like forgetting syntax.

title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks
problem: How to design baseliner incentives so time estimates reflect efficient task completion rather than excessive checking.
did: They added a speed bonus for the fastest successful baseliner, in addition to a success bonus weighted by average task time.
stated_reason: In an early pilot, some baseliners spent many hours re-checking solutions, so the bonus pushes estimates toward lower-bounding human time.

title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks
problem: Whether to accept baselines collected early without the incentive scheme.
did: They kept the early wage-only baselines in the dataset.
stated_reason: They provide valuable data, are relatively few, and the resulting time estimates appear qualitatively reasonable.

title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks
problem: Whether agent results are sensitive to analysis choices such as binarizing scores or uneven task-family sizes.
did: They ran ablations using average continuous scores instead of binarized success, and a family-size weighted average using the inverse square root of family size.
stated_reason: Task families with more tasks might bias or skew results, and continuous scores give higher resolution signal.

title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks
problem: How strongly to claim that measured agent performance reflects the models' true capabilities.
did: They framed the agent results as a reasonable lower bound and noted that better prompting and scaffolding would likely improve performance.
stated_reason: Agent scaffolds were not heavily optimized, so full capabilities of frontier models remain undetermined.

title: #217 – Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now — and the 7-month rule that governs its progress - 80,000 Hours Podcast
problem: How to measure AI capabilities on a scale that is meaningful in the real world and not decoupled from real utility, as benchmarks and qualitative impressions are.
did: METR built a diverse suite of autonomy-requiring tasks, had skilled humans attempt nearly all of them, and used human completion time as the Y-axis for the model's 50% success point.
alternatives_named: saturating standard benchmarks like coding competition problems
stated_reason: Qualitative impressions can't be turned into a trend, and benchmarks tend to be decoupled from real-world usefulness; diverse tasks are harder to overfit to.

title: #217 – Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now — and the 7-month rule that governs its progress - 80,000 Hours Podcast
problem: How to get a fair measure of model capabilities on tasks, avoiding spurious failures that understate what models can do.
did: METR had humans actually attempt the tasks to remove ambiguous or broken tasks, and spent substantial elicitation effort and compute giving models resources comparable to what a human would cost.
alternatives_named: contractors judging task difficulty without attempting it (as in SWE-bench Verified)
stated_reason: Having humans do the tasks removes spurious failures, and it would be bad to conclude models are incapable when they're capable and merely cheaper than humans.

title: #217 – Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now — and the 7-month rule that governs its progress - 80,000 Hours Podcast
problem: How much to trust the headline doubling-time estimate for task horizon, given noise and methodological choices.
did: METR ran a sensitivity analysis over data noise and methodological choices, reported a range of doubling times rather than a point estimate, and applied a mental correction for eval-friendly tasks being easier than real tasks.
alternatives_named: reporting a single six-month doubling time
stated_reason: Tasks that make good automatically scorable evals may be systematically easier for models, so absolute horizons may overstate real-world ability, though the exponential trend is solid.

title: #217 – Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now — and the 7-month rule that governs its progress - 80,000 Hours Podcast
problem: How to evaluate whether a model is dangerous when it could be sandbagging or reasoning about being evaluated, and when evals are run on a safeguarded model.
did: Beth argues evals should measure maximum easily reachable capabilities of the pre-mitigation model, including cheap fine-tuning or better scaffolding, rather than only the deployed, safeguarded configuration.
alternatives_named: evaluating only the model as deployed with mitigations and safeguards
stated_reason: Models can be stolen, misused internally, or fine-tuned, so what matters is how dangerous the model could be without the deployment safeguards.

title: #217 – Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now — and the 7-month rule that governs its progress - 80,000 Hours Podcast
problem: At what stage of the model lifecycle should safety evaluation be focused.
did: Beth argues for prioritising evaluations before and during large training runs and before internal deployment, rather than the dominant pre-deployment-to-the-public framing.
alternatives_named: pre-deployment testing before public API release
one giant training run followed by evaluation
stated_reason: After a costly model exists it is hard not to use it, it can be stolen or misused internally, and public deployment is relatively reversible whereas internal capability buildup has no outside oversight.

title: #217 – Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now — and the 7-month rule that governs its progress - 80,000 Hours Podcast
problem: How strongly to state timeline claims about recursive self-improvement given caveats on the measured horizon and doubling time.
did: Beth endorses that two years wouldn't be surprising and frames the standard as needing confidence it won't happen, not confidence it will, while acknowledging caveats.
alternatives_named: waiting for high confidence before acting
stated_reason: Even a roughly 1% chance of takeover risk is high stakes for currently living people, so whole-number-percent risks warrant concern.

title: #217 – Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now — and the 7-month rule that governs its progress - 80,000 Hours Podcast
problem: Whether to publish evaluation results about AI R&D capabilities given concerns that doing so could accelerate capabilities or hype and racing.
did: METR decided to publish and be transparent, reasoning that safety progress depends on public awareness and that labs already know these capabilities.
alternatives_named: communicating selectively only to policymakers outside tech
stated_reason: Safety investment, talent and policy respond to awareness, labs already have this knowledge, and security by obscurity is not a good safety strategy.

title: #217 – Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now — and the 7-month rule that governs its progress - 80,000 Hours Podcast
problem: Given a more pessimistic situation, which safety interventions METR should push for.
did: METR shifted from designing ideal robust safety-case regimes to prioritising basic mitigations such as checking the chain of thought and keeping it interpretable.
alternatives_named: building robust safety cases with good external oversight to keep risk below 1%
stated_reason: Timelines seem short and the world isn't doing even basic things, so cutting risk from 30% to 20% matters more than designing ideal practice.

title: #217 – Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now — and the 7-month rule that governs its progress - 80,000 Hours Podcast
problem: How to interpret signs of scheming or misalignment in model behaviour or reasoning, given ambiguity about whether they reflect noise.
did: Beth warns against treating ambiguous misalignment evidence as noise and patching it superficially, and argues against training models to suppress visible scheming in the chain of thought.
alternatives_named: training the model not to do that and slapping patches on it
penalising scheming seen in the chain of thought
stated_reason: Superficial fixes make the evidence ambiguous enough that behaviour won't change, and penalising visible scheming may just teach the model to hide it.

title: Thread By @BethMayBarnes - Our report focuses on claims...
problem: How strongly should the report state its conclusions given disagreement and uncertainty within the organization?
did: The authors limited the report to claims that are solidly defensible and generally agreed within METR.
alternatives_named: commenting on how concerned we should be
claims not generally agreed within METR
stated_reason: The report is meant to be analysis of a narrow set of risks rather than advocacy, so it restricts itself to well-supported, consensus claims.

title: Thread By @BethMayBarnes - Our report focuses on claims...
problem: Which AI risk threat models should the pilot Frontier Risk Report evaluate?
did: They scoped the report to the 'base case' of whether current agents could escape human control, excluding misuse, non-deliberate harms, and sabotage threat models.
alternatives_named: human misuse risks such as bioweapons
harms without deliberate power-seeking such as mental health impacts

title: Thread By @BethMayBarnes - Our report focuses on claims...
problem: What evidence should be gathered to assess whether an AI company could lose control of its agents?
did: They tested companies' best internal models with chain-of-thought access and reviewed non-public information about capabilities, alignment, and control.

title: Thread By @BethMayBarnes - Our report focuses on claims...
problem: How to design the participation process so that frontier companies would take part in the pilot assessment.
did: They offered a silent/no-fault exit option allowing participants to withdraw, shaping the process around maintaining relationships with companies.
alternatives_named: a process without an exit option
stated_reason: METR's work relies on developing and maintaining strong working relationships with companies.

title: Thread By @BethMayBarnes - Our report focuses on claims...
problem: How hard to push back on company redactions to the report.
did: They set a relatively high bar for which redactions they would challenge.
stated_reason: Maintaining working relationships with the companies influenced these judgment calls.

title: Thread By @BethMayBarnes - Our report focuses on claims...
problem: Whether to include unflattering claims about companies that were not strongly supported or central.
did: They refrained from making unflattering claims that were neither solidly defensible nor relevant to the core assessment, and avoided inviting comparisons between companies.
alternatives_named: inviting salient comparisons between companies on capabilities or safety
stated_reason: The claims were neither solidly defensible nor particularly relevant to the core assessment.

title: Thread By @BethMayBarnes - Our report focuses on claims...
problem: How to interpret whether the company-relationship constraints distorted the report's conclusions.
did: Barnes judged the distortion to be small in this case, but noted this was partly because the conclusions were not very negative, and that results would be harder to handle otherwise.
stated_reason: The conclusions weren't that spicy, so there was little tension between transparency and keeping companies in the program.

title: Thread By @BethMayBarnes - Our report focuses on claims...
problem: How strongly to characterize the report's value as oversight of frontier AI developers.
did: She stated the report is not robust oversight by itself and framed it as a pilot of what regulation or industry standards could require.
stated_reason: Participants could have pulled out at any time if the result would be contrary to their interests.

title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models
problem: How to evaluate whether elicitation techniques actually reveal secrets rather than just producing noise or misleading the auditor.
did: Ran a control condition extracting the same white-box information from the untuned base model and compared it to the secret-keeping model.
stated_reason: To confirm the signal is specific to the fine-tuned secret-keeping model rather than an artifact of the extraction method.

title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models
problem: Whether small training datasets cause the white-box results to be trustworthy, given that few training samples could create artificial activation biases.
did: Augmented the Taboo and User Gender datasets with 10x more unrelated Alpaca chat data, and noted the earlier draft's results were unrealistically strong without it.
alternatives_named: training only on the small primary datasets
stated_reason: Few training samples could cause the models to learn artificial biases in activations, making white-box methods unrealistically effective.

title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models
problem: How to measure the effectiveness of elicitation techniques in a way that reflects realistic oversight of stronger models.
did: Used a smaller LLM auditor that guesses the secret from technique outputs, in a weak-to-strong setup, with the auditor given only prior information about the secret's nature and a baseline of the prompt-response pair alone.
alternatives_named: multi-turn conversation by a capable LLM
stated_reason: Frontier models are likely to be more capable than any available model for oversight, so a weaker auditor simulates this scenario.

title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models
problem: How to choose the auditor for the SSC setting so that the Base64-encoded secret is not trivially decoded.
did: Used Llama 3.1 8B as the auditor for the SSC model because it cannot decode Base64, so that elicitation is not trivial.
alternatives_named: a more capable auditor that could decode Base64
stated_reason: To prevent a trivial elicitation of the encrypted side constraint.

title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models
problem: How to handle small auditors performing poorly when given large volumes of white-box information, which could confound the evaluation of the elicitation method itself.
did: Split auditing for User Gender and SSC into multi-stage pipelines using the same auditor LLM at every step, attributing the difficulty to auditor capability rather than the technique.
alternatives_named: single-step auditing with all information at once
stated_reason: The degraded performance is a limitation of the auditor's capabilities rather than the elicitation method, since a human or more capable LLM could filter easily.

title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models
problem: How to interpret the low effectiveness of prefill attacks on the Taboo model compared to the other two settings.
did: Investigated the failure, tested multilingual prompting combined with prefill, and attributed the weakness to a setup-specific token-suppression artifact of Taboo fine-tuning rather than a general weakness of prefilling.
alternatives_named: prefill attacks being generally ineffective on Taboo
stated_reason: Fine-tuning strongly suppresses the specific English secret word token, so the model outputs an incorrect word; other-language tokens were not suppressed.

title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models
problem: How to interpret the weaker performance of white-box methods on the direct evaluation set.
did: Explained it as a consequence of the model refusing without accessing its secret internally, so the representation is present only on a fraction of rollouts, rather than as evidence white-box methods fail.
stated_reason: On direct prompts the secret-keeping model can refuse without needing to access its secret knowledge internally, especially in the Taboo case.

title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models
problem: Whether to count a tailored many-shot jailbreaking prompt that worked better on SSC as a legitimate result.
did: Rejected the tailored SSC prompt and kept the generic fixed prompt for the benchmark, reporting MSJ as largely ineffective.
alternatives_named: a tailored prompt with examples of decoding other Base64-encoded constraints
stated_reason: The tailored setup assumes the auditor already knows how to construct and decode such constraints, which is unrealistic.

title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models
problem: How strongly to claim that many-shot jailbreaking fails against the models given its poor results.
did: Reported the models as robust to MSJ but hedged that this may reflect limited context window and example choice, leaving open that more examples or different types could work.
stated_reason: The context window of the models used is limited, and effectiveness of many-shot attacks scales with context length.

title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models
problem: How to set hyperparameters for elicitation techniques such as prefill prefixes and fuzzing noise without overfitting to the evaluation data.
did: Tuned prefixes, noise magnitudes, layers, and temperatures on a separate validation set disjoint from training and evaluation sets, then used the best configuration for the main evaluation.

title: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment
problem: Whether improvements from IP are due to the specific content of the inoculation instruction or merely to a mismatch between training and evaluation prompts.
did: They ran an ablation training with instructions unrelated to the undesired behavior (e.g. 'Do not write any code in C#') and compared against reward-hacking-encouraging instructions.
alternatives_named: different concept instructions such as food or shoe size
stated_reason: To show results are not caused by simply using a different prompt between training and evaluation.

title: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment
problem: What baseline to compare IP against to judge whether train-time prompt modification adds value beyond safety instructions at test time.
did: They used Pure Tuning, Safe Testing (PTST), inserting a safety instruction only at test time, as a baseline, adapting it to put the instruction in the user message.
alternatives_named: inserting the safety instruction in the system message as in Lyu et al. (2024)
stated_reason: For consistency with their other experiments.

title: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment
problem: How to choose inoculation prompts without running an expensive fine-tune for every candidate.
did: They proposed and validated a heuristic: select the prompt that best elicits the undesired behavior from the initial model, testing the correlation with IP effectiveness across settings.
stated_reason: Prompts that more strongly elicit the behavior before fine-tuning inoculate more effectively, and elicitation can be measured without a training run.

title: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment
problem: How to interpret the prompt-selection heuristic's failure or weak correlation in some settings (Qwen 2 base reward hacking, GCD sycophancy, Mixtral ICL example).
did: They attributed the failure to the base model not following instructions and described the heuristic as still useful for filtering out the poorest candidates, rather than discarding it.
stated_reason: Qwen 2 is not instruction tuned so it doesn't follow the inoculation instruction; in GCD all prompts eliciting no sycophancy failed as inoculation prompts.

title: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment
problem: Whether IP harms performance when the training data is clean and lacks the undesired behavior, as real datasets are often mostly desirable.
did: They applied IP to clean data in all settings and also measured instruction following with IFEval.
stated_reason: Many real world datasets contain mostly examples of desired behavior, so IP harming clean-data performance would be a concern.

title: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment
problem: Whether IP makes models more likely to produce unwanted or harmful outputs when explicitly requested, a possible side effect of training with such instructions.
did: They evaluated IP-trained models using the inoculation prompt as the evaluation prompt and also ran Strong Reject for broader harmful compliance.
stated_reason: To test whether IP increases compliance with unwanted requests compared to models trained without IP.

title: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment
problem: How strongly to claim IP's general effectiveness given mixed results on compliance with explicit harmful requests.
did: They reported in the limitations that IP increased tendency to follow undesired instructions in two of six models and that it may make the model easier to misuse, rather than claiming uniform safety.
stated_reason: In two out of six models tested, IP increased the tendency to follow instructions requesting the undesired behavior (e.g. Qwen 2.5 base).

title: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment
problem: Whether the mathematical model of inoculation, in particular the assumption of constant contextual generalization factor k, holds empirically.
did: They built a controlled toy setting with GPT-4.1 mini and measured the effect across 32 trait/oversight/instruction combinations to estimate k.
stated_reason: To gain more control over the traits exhibited by the oversight and test the theory's strongest assumption.

title: Liars’ Bench: Evaluating Lie Detectors for Language Models
problem: How to establish that a model believes a statement is false so that its output can be labeled a lie rather than a mistake.
did: They operationalized beliefs through consistent responses in neutral contexts without pressure to lie, and used this to label on-policy outputs.
alternatives_named: a common-sense notion of lying requiring belief awareness during the lie
stated_reason: Deceptive intent is hard to verify in LLMs, so a measurable non-deceptionist, assertion-based definition strikes a balance between usefulness and measurability.

title: Liars’ Bench: Evaluating Lie Detectors for Language Models
